planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this southern Chinese mayapple relative forms a broad, rounded, deeply lobed leaf that can rival pleianthum and versipelle in scale.

directions: Set out rhizome divisions in fall in rich, consistently moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial to deep shade. Podophyllum majoense is a collector's mayapple from the mountain forests of Guangxi, Guizhou, Hubei, Sichuan, and Yunnan, producing a large, thin, kidney-shaped leaf cut into several lobes, grayish purple beneath and dark green above. Clusters of purple flowers open low on the stem beneath the foliage canopy in spring, followed by oblong red berries in summer. Grow it alongside other Asian mayapples and epimediums where its oversized leaf provides a bold textural contrast, and keep soil evenly moist through summer dormancy preparation.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this high-elevation Tibetan species comes from spruce and fir forest at 2,500-3,500m and prefers a cooler, less humid shade garden than lowland Asian mayapples.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, mimicking the high-elevation conifer forests of Xizang (Tibet) where this mayapple naturally grows. Podophyllum tsayuense is among the taller Asian mayapples, sending up an unbranched, scaly-based stem topped by a pair of large, rounded, palmately cut leaves. Clusters of relatively large white flowers, each several centimeters across, open beneath the foliage in late spring, followed by fleshy berries in summer. Because of its origin in cool, high-elevation forest, it appreciates a shadier, moister site than lowland relatives and benefits from a thick leaf-litter mulch that keeps roots cool through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in sun to semi-shade; this evergreen southern Chinese and Vietnamese species tolerates more light than most Disporum and keeps its glossy foliage year-round in milder climates.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moisture-retentive, fertile soil in a site offering sun to semi-shade; unlike most fairy bells, this evergreen species from southern China and Vietnam holds onto its glossy, pleated, lance-shaped leaves through winter in mild climates. Upright stems branch into arching laterals clothed in dark green foliage, and in late spring clusters of nodding, cream, green-tipped bell flowers appear, maturing into black berries by late summer. Give it a sheltered spot out of hard freezes and consistent moisture during the growing season; it makes a striking textural foil for hostas and ferns where winters are mild enough for its foliage to persist.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in shade to part sun; this Taiwanese endemic is smaller in stature than most fairy bells and best suited to zones without hard, prolonged freezes.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in shade to part sun. Disporum shimadae is a compact fairy bells endemic to the forests and hillsides of northern Taiwan, bearing broad, waxy, lemon-yellow bell flowers with a distinctly flared, open mouth that stand out among its relatives' narrower, paler blooms. Flowering occurs in spring on arching, leafy stems, followed later by berries typical of the genus. Its smaller stature makes it well suited to the front of a shaded border or a woodland container planting, and it is still uncommon in cultivation outside specialist collections, so source plants from a reputable woodland or bulb specialist.
sources: Taxonomic revision of Disporum of Taiwan (PhytoKeys)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this diminutive species from Sichuan's Emei Shan stays noticeably shorter than most garden Solomon's seals, making it suitable for smaller shade plantings.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Polygonatum omeiense is a small-statured Solomon's seal native to forested slopes around Emei Shan in central Sichuan, producing a purple-spotted stem lined with alternate, oblong-lanceolate leaves. In late spring, slender, cylindric, yellowish-white flowers dangle singly or in pairs from the leaf axils, followed by berries typical of the genus. Its diminutive scale compared to larger Solomon's seals like P. odoratum or P. multiflorum makes it a good choice for tucking among rocks or smaller companions in a shaded woodland setting; mulch with leaf litter to retain the cool, humid soil it favors.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
